title: Reformers Yes States Should Intervene in Failing Districts
author: Michael Petrilli
source: Schooled by Mike Petrilli Substack, May 1, 2026
summary: Petrilli convenes a chorus of reformers — Paul Hill, Robin Lake, Christy Wolfe, Anne Wicks, Charlie Barone, Dale Chu — on whether states should intervene in failing districts (not just failing schools), spurred by the Houston and Memphis takeovers. The consensus is yes-and: state takeovers can neutralize the local political opposition that usually defeats school-change efforts, and the toolkit available today (technology, the science of reading, portfolio accountability) is richer than it was 20 years ago when state takeovers were last in fashion. Hill argues many districts will become financial basket cases and states should use that leverage on quality as well as budgets. Lake counters that states have limited authority, staff, and expertise to drive improvement directly and should pressure local action rather than micromanage. Wolfe extends the portfolio frame to ensuring supply of high-quality seats matches demand, citing NOLA. Wicks emphasizes the leadership-and-incentives conditions that made HISD work (Mike Miles plus Texas legislation HB2/SB2/HB3/HB8). Chu warns from his Indiana, Camden, Newark, and Houston experience that governance change is the easiest part — leadership and system-building capacity are the binding constraints, with Third Future Schools' disciplined data-and-execution model as one of the rare external operators that can actually do the work. The piece closes with the new Fordham Institute science-of-reading report, OECD data on the wide US distribution of teacher knowledge, Shavar Jeffries' college-for-all argument and Petrilli's pushback (the wage premium is a college-completion premium, and we shouldn't push the lowest-prepared students into a bet they're likely to lose), Bruno Manno on apprenticeships, and Tim DeRoche on LAUSD's race-based funding formula.
points: State takeovers of failing districts can work because they neutralize the local opposition that usually defeats school-change efforts; the available toolkit (tech, science of reading, portfolio accountability) is richer than 20 years ago.
States have limited authority, staff, and expertise to manage schools directly; Robin Lake argues they should use their power to enable and pressure local action rather than micromanage.

Governance change is the easiest part of takeover — leadership and system-building capacity are the binding constraints (Dale Chu, drawing on Indiana, Camden, Newark, Houston experience), and the Third Future Schools-style disciplined operator pipeline is rare.

Texas's HISD model is replicating through its bench: Daniel Soliz (Fort Worth deputy), Ena Meyers (Lake Worth), Sandi Massey (Beaumont) all came up under Mike Miles — leadership development matters as much as policy for replication.

Petrilli's pushback on Shavar Jeffries' college-for-all argument: the college wage premium is really a college-completion premium, and pushing low-performing students into a bet they're likely to lose is harmful; the right answer is honest advising plus alternative pathways like apprenticeships.
quotes: State takeover or adoption of the portfolio strategy is only an opportunity to execute a strategy for improving the schools available to kids in the locality. State takeover can neutralize opposition that usually defeats school change efforts.

States are constitutionally responsible for education and must step in when localities fail, but they have limited authority, staff, and expertise to actually drive improvement in individual schools. States should use their powers to enable and pressure local action rather than trying to directly manage schools from the state level.

I would love for districts to manage this directly without state takeovers, but I simply don't see school boards ever being willing to do this (or to fully understand the student outcomes and/or teaching and learning enough to make hard but necessary governance choices). Someone has to be the grown-up in the room, and I think that is the state.

I've become convinced that leadership and system-building capacity are the real binding constraints. That's true at the state level with Mike Morath, but just as much at the district level with Mike Miles.

I'm generally encouraged by the direction in Texas and now Tennessee, but I think we should be careful not to understate how complex and contingent state takeover strategies are in practice. The governance change is in many ways the easiest part; sustaining improvement depends on a much deeper set of leadership and system-building conditions than is often acknowledged.

It is a bet. As Shavar writes, the college wage premium remains robust. But it really should be called the 'college completion premium,' because there's little to no benefit for students who try college but drop out before completing a valuable degree or credential.

But the odds of completing college are terrible for students at the other end of the spectrum, with very low test scores, poor grades in easy classes, a spotty attendance record, and a general antipathy toward school. We should not be encouraging such young people to gamble on college attendance.” Archived from Schooled by Mike Petrilli Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
